docs.title: AI for EE Research
docs.text:
Title: AI for EE Research: From Researcher to Orchestrator

Target Audience: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research

Prerequisites:

  • Graduate standing (or equivalent research experience) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, or a related field
  • Working knowledge of at least one programming language, preferably Python
  • Basic comfort with a command line, a text editor, and Git
  • Experience writing a technical paper or report
  • No prior machine learning, prompt engineering, or agent experience required

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Graduate research in electrical engineering and computer design is a pipeline of repeatable tasks: finding and reading literature, brainstorming and scoping a problem, writing analysis and simulation code, processing data, and preparing figures and manuscripts. Generative AI tools and agents can now take a substantial share of each of these tasks, but only for researchers who know how to direct them, check their output, and take responsibility for the results.

This course is a hands-on guide to that skill. Its central idea is a change in the researcher's role: from doing every task personally to orchestrating a team of agents. In the vision developed throughout the book, each researcher coordinates roughly 20 planning agents, which explore literature, decompose problems, and draft specifications, and 10 execution agents, which write code, run analyses, build simulations, and prepare figures and manuscripts. The researcher's job is to set direction, supply domain judgment, resolve conflicts between agents, and decide what is true. The researcher stays accountable for the science.

The course is practical rather than theoretical. Students learn the two building blocks that make agents reliable in a research setting: plain Markdown files that capture a project's goals, conventions, and constraints, and reusable agent skills that turn a repeatable research task into a single, testable command. Throughout, the course works from case studies of real work, including AI-generated interactive simulations (MicroSims), intelligent textbooks, and a full paper prepared for arXiv with AI agents, and it treats effective, creative, responsible, and ethical use as equal goals.

The course also teaches personal knowledge graphs: a researcher's own notes, papers, experiments, people, and projects, represented as linked entities and relationships rather than as a folder of files. A personal knowledge graph gives agents a structured, queryable memory of the researcher's work, and the course shows how to build one with an agent, query it, use it to ground a model's answers, and decide what an agent may be allowed to see.

The course also surveys the new class of always-on personal agents that arrived in 2026, because researchers will meet them in their own labs whether or not a course introduces them. These are hosted or self-hosted agents that keep their own cloud computer, sign in to tools on the user's behalf, remember context across sessions, and work while the researcher is away. As of this writing the survey covers SpaceXAI's Grok Bot, OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse, Anthropic's Claude Cowork, and the open-source OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. The goal is not to rank products, which change monthly, but to give researchers durable criteria for choosing and supervising any of them: where the agent runs, what it can reach, how permissions and approvals work, what it costs, and what happens to research data. The current research notes are collected in the appendix Personal Agents.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
1. The research workflow and where AI helps: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, coding, and manuscript preparation
  2. How large language models work, at the level a researcher needs: tokens, context windows, hallucination, model selection, and cost
  3. Prompting and context engineering for research tasks
  4. Markdown as a project knowledge format: project instruction files, notes, specifications, and conventions that agents read before they work
  5. Agent skills: designing, writing, testing, and sharing reusable skills for repeatable research tasks
  6. Agents and tool use: file access, shell commands, web search, subagents, hooks, and connecting to external tools and data
  7. Planning agents and execution agents: dividing work, handoffs, and coordination
  8. Orchestration: the researcher as the coordinator of 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents
  9. AI-assisted literature search, reading, and synthesis
  10. AI-assisted data analysis and scientific coding, including scripts for simulation, signal processing, and plotting
  11. AI-assisted brainstorming, problem framing, and hypothesis development
  12. AI-assisted manuscript preparation: structure, LaTeX, figures, references, and arXiv submission
  13. Interactive simulations (MicroSims) and intelligent textbooks as ways to communicate and teach research results
  14. Verification, validation, and reproducibility of AI-assisted work
  15. Responsible and ethical use: citation, disclosure, privacy, intellectual property, bias, and academic integrity
  16. Case studies of AI-assisted research and publication workflows, including the MicroSims arXiv paper and intelligent textbook projects
  17. Personal agents: always-on hosted and self-hosted agents such as Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent, including their architectures, permission and approval models, multi-agent features, pricing, and data-handling trade-offs
  18. Personal knowledge graphs: representing a researcher's notes, papers, and projects as entities and relationships, building them with agents, querying them, using them as grounded agent memory, and protecting their privacy

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Training, fine-tuning, or building large language models from scratch
  • Machine learning theory, deep learning architectures, and neural network mathematics
  • AI hardware design, accelerators, and chip architecture for AI workloads
  • Vendor-specific electronic design automation (EDA) flows and tool tutorials
  • Domain-specific EE theory such as circuit analysis, device physics, or quantum electronics (the course assumes students bring this knowledge)
  • Legal advice on copyright, patent, and data-protection law
  • Comparative benchmarking and rankings of commercial AI products
  • Using AI to replace the researcher's judgment, authorship, or accountability

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • Define the key terms: token, context window, prompt, agent, subagent, skill, tool call, hallucination, and orchestration
  • List the five everyday research tasks this course targets: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, coding, and manuscript preparation
  • Recall the purpose of a project instruction file and the typical sections it contains
  • Identify the parts of an agent skill: name, description, instructions, and supporting files
  • Name common failure modes of AI output, including fabricated citations, silent errors in code, and overconfident summaries
  • State the difference between a planning agent and an execution agent
  • Name the major personal agent products (Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent) and the vendor or project behind each

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain why a language model can produce fluent but false statements
  • Describe how context window limits affect long research tasks
  • Explain why Markdown is a good format for knowledge that both humans and agents read
  • Summarize how an agent differs from a chatbot, and how tool use extends what it can do
  • Describe how an always-on personal agent differs from a session-based assistant, including where it runs, how it signs in to tools, and how it keeps memory between sessions
  • Explain how a personal knowledge graph differs from a folder of notes, and how entities, relationships, and backlinks make a researcher's knowledge queryable by an agent
  • Explain how splitting work between planning and execution agents reduces errors and cost
  • Describe the researcher's responsibilities when AI contributes to a result, including citation and disclosure

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Write a project instruction file that gives an agent the goals, conventions, and constraints of a research project
  • Use an AI tool to run a literature search and produce an annotated reading list with verified citations
  • Prompt an agent to write, run, and debug an analysis script on a real dataset
  • Create a reusable agent skill that automates one repeatable task from their own research workflow
  • Use an agent to draft a manuscript section from notes, then revise it into their own voice
  • Generate an interactive simulation that illustrates a concept from their research
  • Build a personal knowledge graph from their own research notes and papers using an agent for entity extraction, then query it to ground an agent's answers

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Decompose a research project into tasks suited to planning agents and tasks suited to execution agents
  • Compare the output of several agents on the same task and identify where and why they disagree
  • Trace an error in AI-generated code or a claim in AI-generated text back to its source
  • Distinguish tasks that benefit from AI assistance from tasks that require the researcher's direct work
  • Analyze a case study of an AI-assisted research project and map its workflow, handoffs, and review points
  • Compare personal agents on architecture, permission and approval model, multi-agent support, integrations, and cost, separating vendor claims from independently tested behavior

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Verify AI-generated citations, numerical results, and code against primary sources and independent tests
  • Judge whether an AI-assisted result meets the standard for reproducibility in their field
  • Assess a skill or agent workflow for reliability, cost, and risk before relying on it
  • Critique an AI-assisted manuscript for accuracy, originality, and proper attribution
  • Decide when and how to disclose AI assistance to a venue, advisor, or collaborator under ethical and institutional guidelines
  • Assess the security and data-handling risks of giving a personal agent access to research accounts, unpublished data, and licensed tools before adopting it
  • Decide which parts of a personal knowledge graph an agent may read, and assess the privacy risk of exposing unpublished results through it

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design an orchestrated team of planning and execution agents for a research project, with defined roles, handoffs, and review checkpoints
  • Build a personal library of agent skills and project instruction files for their research group
  • Produce a complete, verified research artifact with agent assistance, such as a literature review, an analysis notebook, or a draft paper
  • Develop a responsible-use policy for AI in their lab or research group
  • Capstone project: plan and run an end-to-end research task with a coordinated team of agents, document the workflow, and present the verified results along with an honest account of where human judgment was required

docs.title: List of Appendices
docs.text:
The appendices hold supporting research that is not yet part of a chapter. They are working notes and will be revised as the book develops.

  1. Personal Agents - Research notes, gathered in October 2026, on always-on personal AI agents: SpaceXAI's Grok Bot, OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse, Anthropic's Claude Cowork, and the open-source OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. It compares their architecture, permission models, multi-agent features, pricing, and open questions, and notes that most claims are vendor-stated with no independent testing.
  2. Personal Knowledge Graphs - A summary of Dan McCreary's prior research on personal knowledge graphs (PKGs) and how to integrate them securely into an organization's collective knowledge. docs.title: Appendix: Personal Agents
docs.text:
Research notes — not yet a finished chapter

This appendix holds raw research gathered on October 15, 2026. Nearly every claim is vendor-stated or comes from press coverage; we found no independent benchmarks or controlled tests of any product listed here. Prices, tiers, and features changed several times within weeks of launch, so verify against each vendor's own pages before relying on a number.

docs.title: Why this matters for EE research
docs.text: A personal agent is an AI system that does not just answer a question but carries out multi-step work on your behalf — signing in to tools, running routines, and coming back when it is done or needs a decision. For a researcher, that could mean overnight literature sweeps, rerunning an analysis when new lab data lands, or filing bug tickets against a simulation toolchain. The products below all arrived within roughly two months of each other in mid-2026, so the category is moving fast.

docs.title: Grok Bot (SpaceXAI)
docs.text: SpaceXAI announced Grok Bot on August 11, 2026, as an early-beta, cloud-based agent service. "Bot" is the product name; it is not the ordinary Grok chatbot. It appears to be the first joint product of xAI and Cursor. Sources disagree on whether SpaceX is acquiring Cursor or merging with it (MacRumors cites a $60 billion acquisition), so treat the deal terms as unsettled.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Persistent cloud computer. Each user gets a cloud machine with a browser, files, and a terminal. Work continues when the user's laptop is off.
  • Signs in like a human. Bots log in to websites and apps, including services that offer no API or MCP integration.
  • Teachable routines. A user shows a bot a task once; it saves the routine and later runs it on its own.
  • Multiple bots. Several bots can share one group chat, share context, and hand work to each other. A manager bot can delegate to specialist bots. AIMultiple reports up to six bots per group chat and "Team Bots" on Teams/Enterprise plans (public beta since September 28).
  • Memory. Bots keep memory across conversations and may start work "before you need to ask," per SpaceXAI.
  • Interface. Work is assigned in a chat window on desktop or iOS. The bot returns a result or asks for approval.

SpaceXAI's own example uses include updating a CRM from call transcripts, onboarding new hires and processing invoices in Gmail, and reproducing a bug, filing a ticket, and handing the fix to a debugging bot.

docs.title: Security claims and open questions
docs.text:
SpaceXAI states that Grok Bot uses Cursor SSO and authentication, privacy mode, encryption in transit and at rest, a training opt-out, and an "Auto Review" step for sensitive actions. Enterprise admins can configure data-loss prevention, certificates, proxies, and network controls.

Open questions raised by analysts:

  • Shared logins. Isolation is per user, not per bot. All of a user's bots share one computer, including its files, browser, and logins, so one compromised bot exposes the rest.
  • Undocumented details. Retention defaults, credential handling, permission granularity, audit records, which actions need approval by default, and whether memory can be viewed or edited.
  • Reliability. Nothing documents failure handling or what happens to a saved routine when a website's interface changes.
  • Cost surprises. Cursor itself warns that an hourly routine or a busy Slack trigger "can use a week of usage in a day."

docs.title: Dots (OpenAI)
docs.text:
OpenAI introduced Dots at DevDay on September 29, 2026, as a personal agent inside ChatGPT, powered by GPT-6 Astra.

  • Always-on. A dot runs in the background with its own cloud computer and browser, pursuing goals with minimal oversight.
  • App ecosystem. It can use the 4,000+ apps already connected to ChatGPT and can delegate coding to Codex.
  • Visibility. The user can open a dot's "computer" at any time to see what it is doing, and can connect a dot to their own PC.
  • Communication. A dot can message or call the user with progress, questions, or decisions. Slack and Microsoft Teams integrations were announced; text-message support is described as coming later.
  • Safety model. Passwords used for sign-in are not exposed to the underlying model. Proactive background research uses read-only app access. Dots have built-in rules for when to act versus ask, and users can write custom approval rules. OpenAI says it is working with Microsoft to bring Dots under Agent 365 security controls.
  • One dot for now. Each eligible user gets one primary dot they can name and customize. OpenAI says it expects "teams of Dots working together," but multi-dot control is not available at launch.
  • Availability. Launched for Pro and Business Premium users in "eligible markets"; reports differ on whether Business and Enterprise are included, and some exclude the EEA, Switzerland, and the UK for personal accounts.

Conflicting price reports

Engadget reports the first dot is free for Pro and Business Premium subscribers. AIMultiple lists a $100/mo starting price. We could not reconcile the two; check OpenAI's own announcement.

TechCrunch notes that much of what Dots do was already possible with Codex and similar agent harnesses — Dots package those capabilities around independent action.

docs.title: Muse (Meta)
docs.text:
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the U.S. for users 18 and older, as a separate app that also runs inside WhatsApp. It is aimed at everyday tasks: schedules, shopping, travel, and turning long-term goals into plans.

  • Architecture. Each user's agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine.
  • Permissions. A layer called Sentinel decides whether each connected-app action and outbound request is allowed, blocked, or sent for approval. Meta says the agent never sees your actual passwords or payment details, and each purchase needs approval showing exact details.
  • Visibility. Users can watch the agent's browser as it works and review an activity log.
  • Memory. Stored as editable text files.
  • Pricing. Free tier, plus $20/mo (Power) and $100/mo (Maximum) tiers with weekly token allowances.
  • Privacy. Training on user data is on by default, with an opt-out.
  • Integrations. Centered on Meta's platforms plus email, calendar, payments, and a handful of consumer categories — narrower than the developer-oriented tools.

docs.title: Claude Cowork (Anthropic)
docs.text:
Cowork launched in January 2026 and became generally available on April 9, 2026. It lives in a tab inside Claude Desktop, where Claude reads your files, runs multi-step tasks, and uses plugins and MCP connectors.

  • Platforms. macOS first, with Windows following in February 2026. Anthropic's download page also lists Linux and ChromeOS builds.
  • Scheduled tasks. Added February 25, 2026. A March 2026 source says they require the computer to be awake and Claude Desktop open, which makes Cowork the least "always-on" of the commercial products. That may have changed since.
  • Dispatch. Lets you assign a task from your phone.
  • Pricing. No separate SKU: it is included in Claude Pro ($20/mo), Max ($100 or $200/mo), Team, and Enterprise plans. Agentic tasks reportedly burn usage allowances five to twenty times faster than ordinary chat, and the usage pool is shared with Claude chat and Claude Code.
  • Enterprise. Role-based access control, per-group spend limits, and usage analytics. One source notes Cowork activity is not yet captured in audit logs or the Compliance API.

docs.title: Open-source alternatives: OpenClaw and Hermes Agent
docs.text:
• OpenClaw is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted agent that lives in chat apps such as WhatsApp, Telegram, and Discord. You choose the model (Claude, GPT, Gemini, or a local model through Ollama). Model usage is the main cost — one estimate is $5–50/month. Reviews report reliability problems: runaway loops, malicious skills, and unattended deletions.
  • Hermes Agent (Nous Research, public since February 25, 2026) is also MIT-licensed. It runs on a laptop, server, or cloud sandbox, supports many model providers, and has a learning loop that writes its own skills. The trade-off is that you manage your own servers, secrets, and security.

Press describes Grok Bot as "a user friendly OpenClaw": the same idea, hosted and managed, in exchange for openness and control.

docs.title: Contrast: what actually differs
docs.text:
• Grok Bot's differentiator is the manager/specialist bot model. OpenAI says multi-dot control is planned but not shipped; Muse is one agent per user.
  • Grok Bot is the least transparent. Models are undisclosed, usage allowances are unpublished, and the shared-login design widens the blast radius of any one failure. Dots and Muse document their approval rules more explicitly.
  • Dots lean on the ChatGPT ecosystem — its apps, Codex, and voice calls.
  • Muse targets consumers, with the strongest purchase-approval story but the narrowest work-tool integrations.
  • Cowork is session-oriented and the most mature knowledge-work tool, but the least autonomous.
  • OpenClaw and Hermes trade convenience for control: you pick the model and own the security.

docs.title: Caveats and gaps
docs.text:
• No independent testing. AIMultiple's comparison reports no benchmarks or controlled tests of Dots, Grok Bot, or Muse; the only first-hand evidence is the author's anecdotal use of Grok Bot.
  • Moving prices. Tiers and prices changed within weeks of each launch.
  • Beta status. SpaceXAI's October 12 pages checked by Kingy.ai do not say whether Grok Bot is still in beta.
  • Source bias. Many comparison blogs host or sell one of the products they rank.
  • Unread source. The Neowin article returned HTTP 403 and was not read directly.
  • Cowork currency. The newest Cowork source we found is from August 2026.

docs.title: Questions to resolve before this becomes a chapter
docs.text:
1. Which of these agents suits an EE research workflow (long simulations, licensed EDA tools, lab data) — and which cannot reach those tools at all?
  2. What is each agent's behavior on sensitive or unpublished research data (training defaults, retention, memory)?
  3. How should a research group audit what an always-on agent did overnight?
  4. Which claims can the author verify first-hand with a hands-on trial?

docs.title: The thesis
docs.text: High-quality personal AI agents need access to a person's notes, and the best place to keep notes is a personal knowledge graph (PKG): concepts stored as nodes, with the relationships between them stored as links. The hard part is not the single-user case. It is integrating many individual PKGs into an organization's collective knowledge, which the author calls an integrated personal knowledge graph (IPKG), without losing the speed of personal note taking or exposing knowledge to the wrong people. The research focuses on how to do that securely.

docs.title: What we mean by knowledge
docs.text:
Before a graph can hold knowledge, we need a working definition of it. The Knowledge Triangle shows three layers of increasing value. Raw data is the largest volume but has the lowest meaning. Information is isolated facts extracted from that data. Knowledge is facts connected by meaningful relationships, which is exactly what a graph stores. Hover over each layer for a description.

Run the Knowledge Triangle MicroSim fullscreen

The sim is hosted in the author's Introduction to Graph Databases book, where it has its own lesson page.

docs.title: Where PKGs came from
docs.text:
The chapter traces PKGs through a lineage of ideas for linking notes:

  1. Zettelkasten, the 1500s linked index-card system built on one concept per card and explicit links between concepts.
  2. Hypermedia and hypertext in the 1960s, then HTML and the World Wide Web.
  3. The Semantic Web in 2001, which added relationship types to links.
  4. Electronic note-taking tools such as outliners, mind maps, and Evernote.
  5. Markdown in 2004, a lightweight format that any text editor can produce.
  6. Tools such as Roam Research and Obsidian, which combine hyperlinks, Markdown, and graphs.

The author's point is that Markdown matters: it is why notes can survive changes of tool, which is the same reason this book uses Markdown for project knowledge.

docs.title: Why people use PKGs
docs.text:
The chapter lists five advantages that practitioners report:

  • Quickly organize thoughts. Typing [[ turns a phrase into a node, and autocomplete shows whether the concept already exists.
  • Lower cognitive load. Notes are linked to existing knowledge as they are taken, so the PKG acts as a "second brain" that offloads memory.
  • Non-linear thinking. Concepts connect in any order instead of in the fixed order of sections in a document.
  • Long-term persistence. Plain Markdown outlasts the tools used to edit it.
  • Breaking writer's block. Small subgraphs grow over time, like a "digital garden of ideas."

docs.title: Limits of the tools
docs.text: The chapter also names real problems at the time of writing: sharing a subgraph with others is crude import and export, graph visualization is limited, relationships are untyped, and tools have no fine-grained role-based access control. It raises an ownership question too. A "personal" graph of work knowledge overlaps with an employer's intellectual property.

docs.title: The free-form versus structured tension
docs.text:
The central design tension is between fast, free-form personal note taking and the consistent structure an organization needs to reuse knowledge.

Free form Structured No rules, quick and easy Many rules, slow but consistent Low semantics High semantics Hard to validate and query Easy to validate and query Example: Notepad Example: Wikipedia Infobox

The chapter places tools on a spectrum from Notepad and wikis, through PKGs, to ontology editors such as Protege and graph databases such as Neo4j and TigerGraph, with a not-yet-built "ML-PKG" that uses machine learning to suggest links as you type.

Two ideas follow from this tension:

  • Typed versus untyped links. A wiki links pages of a single type with a single relationship ("is related to"). A true knowledge graph gives each node and edge a type, which is what makes it queryable. The author cites Jim Hendler's hypothesis that "a little semantics goes a long way."
  • Name uniqueness and aliases. PKGs should refuse duplicate concept names, offer to merge on rename, and support aliases, which many tools do poorly.

docs.title: Making integration feel fast
docs.text:
The practical recipe is to extend the as-you-type loop with organizational knowledge instead of adding forms:

  • Trigger characters such as [[, @ (people), and # (tags), plus prefixes such as g: for a company glossary, pull suggestions from enterprise lists.
  • Monitor the acceptance rate of suggestions and aim for 30% or higher before wide rollout, or users will turn the feature off.
  • Link to permalinks (PURLs) rather than file paths, and monitor for broken links, because broken links erode trust.
  • Use bidirectional links so renaming a concept updates every reference. The author's rule of thumb is that about 60% of a knowledge graph's value is in its nodes and 40% in its relationships.
  • Run NLP in real time (entity extraction, classification), within roughly 100 ms, so suggestions do not interrupt typing.
  • Expect to write converters, because each tool extends Markdown differently.

docs.title: Steps to integrate PKGs into the enterprise
docs.text:
The chapter proposes the IPKG hypothesis: users of integrated PKGs will create more valuable knowledge than users of siloed note-taking tools. It then gives a roll-out plan:

  1. Align benefits with the organization's strategy (sharing knowledge, avoiding duplication, consistency, collaboration, productivity, search).
  2. Find an executive sponsor.
  3. Define metrics that a non-specialist can understand, starting with simple features such as shared spell-check dictionaries and automatic hyperlinking of glossary terms.
  4. Inventory existing knowledge repositories (glossaries, product catalogs, employee names, wiki pages, system lists).
  5. Draw a reference architecture diagram with sources on the left, the IPKG in the middle, and consumers on the right.

docs.title: Controlling access
docs.text:
Access control is easy for one person and hard for an organization. The chapter defines the vocabulary (vertex, subgraph, the public graph, roles, access types such as read, rename, move, update and delete, authentication, authorization) and recommends a role-based model:

  • Grant permissions to roles and named groups, not to individuals, so access does not need to change every time someone moves teams.
  • Let people create shared subgraphs with their own permissions.
  • Treat the ontology management problem carefully: low-level changes such as fixing a typo are cheap, but changes to upper ontologies ripple into downstream consumers and need version control and regression tests.
  • Expect merge conflicts. Copying a page from a private graph into a shared one breaks the links that depended on private concepts, so it is often better to create the concept in the shared context in the first place.

Welcome, and Meet Your Guide

Hello, I'm Volt, a border collie, and I will be your guide through this book. Border collies are patient and precise, and I always want to know how a result could be checked. Trust, but verify! Here is exactly what I do in every chapter:

  1. Welcome: I open a chapter and tell you why it is worth your time.
  2. Think: I mark an idea worth pausing on, one that should change how you think.
  3. Tip: I hand you a shortcut you can use right away.
  4. Warn: I flag a trap that catches many researchers, along with the way out.
  5. Encourage: I tell you when a topic is genuinely hard and how to approach it.
  6. Celebrate: I close a chapter by naming what you can now do.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter.

docs.title: Research as a Workflow
docs.text:
A research career is often described in terms of insight, but the day-to-day reality of a graduate student, postdoc, or faculty member is dominated by procedure. A question is chosen, literature is read, an experiment or simulation is designed, data are collected and cleaned, results are analyzed, and a manuscript is written, revised, and submitted. Each of these activities has inputs, outputs, and recognizable quality criteria. The research workflow is this sequence of repeatable activities by which a research question is turned into a validated, communicated result. Naming it matters because anything that can be described as a procedure with checkable outputs can, at least in part, be delegated, and it is precisely this procedural layer that generative AI and agents now handle with useful competence.

Two properties of a workflow make it the right unit of analysis for this book. First, a workflow has stages, and each stage consumes the output of the stage before it. Second, a workflow has handoffs, the points at which one activity ends and another begins, and handoffs are where quality is either confirmed or silently lost. When you work alone and by hand, you carry the handoffs in your head. When part of the workflow is performed by an AI system, the handoffs become explicit artifacts: a file, a prompt, a log, a table of results. Making them explicit is the first practical skill this course teaches.

Real workflows are not straight lines. Analysis that produces a surprising number sends you back to re-examine the measurement, a reviewer's comment sends you back to the analysis, and a new paper in the literature sends you back to the question. These loops are where much of the time in research is actually spent, and they matter for AI use in a specific way: every loop is another chance for a model to introduce an error, and another place where a stale artifact can be mistaken for a current one. A workable discipline is to give every handoff artifact a name, a date, and a note of which earlier artifact it was derived from, so that when a loop is traversed the downstream artifacts known to be stale can be identified at once. In the running example, a change to the record length in the measurement procedure invalidates every ENOB value computed under the old procedure, and the naming convention is what lets you list them.

To keep the discussion concrete, this chapter uses one running example, which is illustrative and not drawn from any published study. A doctoral student is designing a low-power successive-approximation-register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC) for battery-powered sensor nodes, and must show whether the design meets a resolution target. Table 1 follows that project through the workflow.

Stage Input Output Typical handoff artifact Find what is known A topic and a gap in understanding Annotated list of relevant papers Reading list with citations Frame the question Reading list and a design goal One falsifiable research question Question statement Build and measure Question and a design Simulated and measured output records Netlists, scripts, raw data files Analyze Raw data files Quantified results with uncertainty Result tables and plots Communicate Result tables and plots A paper, thesis chapter, or talk Manuscript source and figures

Table 1. The running example's workflow, with the artifact passed between stages.

A Workflow Is a Chain of Evidence

Notice that every stage trusts the one before it. An error in the reading list or in a raw data file does not stay put; it travels to the paper. Ask of every stage: what would reveal a mistake here, before the next stage inherits it?

docs.title: Framing the Research Question
docs.text:
Every downstream activity in the workflow is bounded by the research question: a precise, answerable statement of what the researcher wants to find out. A good question has four properties. It is specific, naming the system and the quantity of interest. It is measurable, so that a result can be compared with a number. It is bounded, limited to conditions that can actually be tested. And it is falsifiable, so that a plausible experiment could show it to be wrong.

The reason this matters more with AI than without it is that generative systems respond fluently to almost any input. A vague question does not produce a visibly vague answer; it produces a confident, well-organized answer to a question you did not quite ask. Precision in the question is therefore the cheapest quality control available.

Weak question Why it fails Stronger question "Make the ADC better." No quantity, no threshold, no condition "Can a 10-bit charge-redistribution SAR ADC in a 65 nm process reach an effective number of bits (ENOB) of at least 9.5 at 1 MS/s while drawing less than 50 µW?" "Is machine learning useful for circuit design?" Unbounded; no test could end the argument "Does a surrogate model trained on 5,000 simulated samples predict the op-amp gain within 1 dB on held-out designs?" "Study noise in the amplifier." Names a topic, not a question "Is the input-referred noise of the low-noise amplifier below 2 nV/√Hz between 1 and 10 MHz at room temperature?"

Table 2. Weak and strong forms of the same research intent. All values are illustrative.

A worked example shows the effect on an agent. Suppose you ask an assistant, "Help me evaluate my ADC." It may produce a plausible list of metrics, a generic evaluation plan, and a recommendation to simulate corners. None of it is wrong, and none of it tells you whether your design met anything. Given the strong version of the question in the first row of Table 2, the same assistant can state the evidence required (a measured ENOB with a stated input frequency and record length), propose the analysis, and tell you when the target has been missed. The question supplied the stopping rule.

The same technique works in reverse: ask an assistant to attack your question rather than answer it. A prompt such as "List the ways this question could be answered yes without the design being useful, and the ways it could be answered no for reasons unrelated to the design" tends to expose hidden conditions, such as the input amplitude, the temperature, or the process corner, that the question left unstated. In the ADC example it exposes that an ENOB of at least 9.5 bits is meaningless without a stated input frequency and amplitude, which sends you back to add them. The assistant is useful here as an adversary, not as an oracle.

Write the Stopping Rule First

Before you open any AI tool, write your question as one sentence containing a metric and a threshold. If an agent cannot tell when it is done, neither can you.

docs.title: The Setting: Electrical Engineering Research
docs.text:
Electrical engineering research is the investigation of circuits, devices, signals, systems, and the computation that runs on them, using theory, simulation, fabrication, and measurement together. Several features of the field shape how AI helps and where it is dangerous.

First, the work is quantitative and the quantities have physical meaning. A number carries units, a measurement condition, and an uncertainty, and a plausible-looking number with the wrong units is worse than no number. Second, the field is tool-dense: circuit simulators, hardware description languages, layout and verification tools, signal analyzers, and a long tail of scripts glue them together, so much of the daily work is writing and debugging code. Third, cycles are slow and expensive. A fabrication run can take months and cost real money, so an error caught in simulation is cheap and the same error caught after tape-out may be unrecoverable. Fourth, the evidence is partly physical: a measurement taken on a bench cannot be regenerated by a model, and a model must never be allowed to stand in for it.

These features make the field both a good fit and a hazardous one for AI assistance. They make it a good fit because so much of the work is structured, scripted, and checkable against physical law. They make it hazardous because the cost of an undetected error is high and the evidence is often irreproducible without the original hardware.

The ADC example gives a feel for the arithmetic you will routinely ask an agent to perform and must be able to check. The effective number of bits relates a measured signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR), expressed in decibels, to an equivalent ideal resolution:

\[ \text{ENOB} = \frac{\text{SNDR}_{\text{dB}} - 1.76}{6.02} \]

Suppose a bench measurement of the example converter gives an SNDR of 57.5 dB. Then ENOB = (57.5 − 1.76) / 6.02 = 55.74 / 6.02 ≈ 9.26 bits. Against the question in Table 2, which required at least 9.5 bits, the design does not yet meet its target. The number is small, the units are explicit, and the conclusion follows directly. This is the style of claim the rest of the book teaches you to delegate drafting of, and never to accept unchecked.

Feature of EE research Where AI helps Where it is hazardous Quantitative results with units Unit conversion, formula implementation, plotting Silent unit or scaling errors that look plausible Tool-dense workflows Writing and debugging scripts and netlists Code that runs but computes the wrong thing Slow, costly fabrication Exploring many designs in simulation first Over-trusting simulation that was never validated against hardware Physical evidence Drafting analysis of measured data you supply Any output presented as a measurement that was not measured

Table 3. Where the field's features create both opportunity and risk.

docs.title: The Five Everyday Research Tasks
docs.text: Across fields and career stages, the procedural work of research reduces to five recurring tasks. This book is organized around them, and each later part of the course returns to one in depth. The sections below define each task and show one concrete place where an AI system fits.

docs.title: Literature Search
docs.text:
Literature search is the systematic discovery of prior work relevant to a question, including the choice of search terms, the databases to query, and the triage of results. Its output is a set of sources the researcher is prepared to cite and defend. AI changes the first half of the task most: generating alternative terminology, expanding abbreviations, and summarizing abstracts. It does not change the second half, which is deciding what is relevant and ensuring the citations are real.

As a worked example, you might ask an assistant to propose search strings for the ADC question. Before the example, note what the prompt contains: a role, the research question, the target databases, and the output format. Specifying all four makes the output directly usable.

You are helping with a literature search in analog circuit design.
Question: Can a 10-bit charge-redistribution SAR ADC in 65 nm reach an
ENOB of at least 9.5 at 1 MS/s below 50 microwatts?
Give 10 Boolean search strings for IEEE Xplore, each using different
terminology (for example "successive approximation" and "SAR"). Return
a table with columns: string, what it targets.

The returned strings are hypotheses about vocabulary, not results. You run them, and you judge which sources are worth reading.

The second half of the task needs a deliberate habit. Each source an assistant mentions should be located in a bibliographic database by title or DOI before it is read, and a source you cannot locate is treated as nonexistent regardless of how plausible it sounds. Once a verified source is in hand, its reference list and the papers that cite it are the most reliable way to widen the search, a technique called citation chaining that later chapters automate. The AI contribution is speed in the first pass; the verification step is what makes the pass trustworthy.

docs.title: Data Analysis
docs.text:
Data analysis is the transformation of raw measurements or simulation output into quantified evidence, usually by cleaning, transforming, visualizing, and testing. In electrical engineering it often means spectral analysis of sampled signals, statistical characterization of noise and mismatch, and comparison of measured results against models. It is the place where agents most often produce silent errors, because an analysis script nearly always runs and produces a number.

A worked example makes the point. To measure ENOB, the converter is driven with a sine wave, a record of N = 4096 output samples is captured at a sampling rate of 1 MS/s, and an FFT is computed. For the spectrum to show a single clean tone, the input frequency should be coherent: an integer number of cycles M in the record, with M and N sharing no common factor. Choosing M = 1021 gives an input frequency of

\[ f_{\text{in}} = \frac{M}{N} f_s = \frac{1021}{4096} \times 1\,\text{MS/s} \approx 249.27\ \text{kHz}. \]

An agent asked to "compute the ENOB from this record" may apply a window function to a record that was already coherent, which spreads signal energy and lowers the apparent SNDR by an amount that depends on the window. The script runs, the number looks reasonable, and the result is wrong by a fraction of a bit. Catching it requires knowing that a coherent record needs no window. That knowledge is yours, and it is exactly the kind of domain judgment that cannot be delegated.

Analysis step What an agent can do What you must check Load and clean the record Parse files, handle missing samples That the sampling rate and units were read correctly Transform Write and run the FFT Windowing and coherence assumptions Quantify Compute SNDR and ENOB The formula, the signal bin, and the noise bins included Visualize Produce plots Axis units, scales, and that the plot shows the data and not a smoothed version

Table 4. Division of labor for the spectral analysis of an ADC record.

A single ENOB value is also an incomplete result. Repeated measurements of the same converter under nominally identical conditions vary, and a claim such as "ENOB = 9.26" means little without a statement of spread. With eight repeated records and a sample standard deviation of 0.05 bits (illustrative), the reported figure becomes 9.26 ± 0.05 bits, and the 9.5-bit target is missed by roughly five standard deviations, a stronger statement than a single number could support. An agent asked only for "the ENOB" will usually return one value. Asking explicitly for the number of records, the mean, and the spread is a small change in the request that changes the quality of the evidence.

docs.title: Brainstorming
docs.text:
Brainstorming is the generation and early filtering of candidate ideas, framings, and approaches before commitment. Generative models are well suited to it because breadth is cheap and a poor suggestion costs only the seconds spent rejecting it. A worked example: asked for alternative architectures that could meet the ADC target, an assistant might list a pipelined converter, a delta-sigma modulator, a time-interleaved SAR, and a hybrid. Your task is to apply what you know about the power budget, the process, and the bandwidth to discard most of them. The assistant widened the set; you chose within it.

Two modes are worth separating, because they need different prompts. Divergent prompts ask for breadth and suspend judgment: "list ten architectures that could, in principle, reach this resolution at this power, including unconventional ones." Convergent prompts apply constraints and ask for ranking with reasons: "rank these against a 50 µW budget, a 65 nm process, and a six-month schedule, and state what you assumed." Running them in that order, in separate prompts, keeps the model from discarding options prematurely. A familiar hazard is anchoring: the first idea an assistant offers tends to shape the rest of the session, including your own thinking. Write down your own three candidates before you ask, and then compare, so that the model's list tests your thinking instead of replacing it.

docs.title: Scientific Coding
docs.text:
Scientific coding is the writing of programs to model, simulate, and analyze physical systems. For many researchers it consumes more hours than any other task, and it is the task for which AI assistants are most mature. The central practical technique is to give generated code a test oracle, a case whose correct answer you know independently.

For the ADC analysis, a perfect quantizer provides one. An ideal N-bit converter driven by a full-scale sine wave has \( \text{SNDR} = 6.02N + 1.76 \) dB, so an ideal 10-bit quantizer should yield 6.02 × 10 + 1.76 = 61.96 dB. If a generated analysis script, fed the output of an ideal 10-bit quantizer, reports 58 dB or 66 dB, the script is wrong, whatever it appears to do. The test costs a few lines and removes a large class of silent errors.

A test oracle is one of three habits that together make generated code trustworthy. The second is boundary testing: feeding the script a record of all zeros, a record with a single sample, and a record of the wrong length, and confirming that it fails loudly instead of returning a number. The third is reading the code before running it on real data, because AI-written scripts often contain defensible-looking choices, such as a default window, a hard-coded sampling rate, or an off-by-one error when excluding the DC bin, that change a result by a fraction of a bit and are visible only in the source. These checks take minutes. They are also the habits that carry over unchanged when the code is written by an agent that ran it itself, a case Chapter 13 treats at length.

docs.title: Manuscript Preparation
docs.text:
Manuscript preparation is the conversion of results into a paper, thesis chapter, or report: structuring the argument, drafting text, producing figures, formatting references, and satisfying the requirements of a venue. It is the stage where AI help is most visible, because fluent drafting is what language models do best, and the stage where the stakes of an unchecked error are highest, because the text will carry your name.

Consider a worked example. You supply a results table in which the measured ENOB is 9.26 bits, and ask an assistant to draft the abstract. The draft states that the converter "achieves nearly 10-bit resolution." The statement is a rounding-up of a number that fell short of the 9.5-bit target in your own question. It reads well and is unsupported. Every number and every adjective in AI-drafted text is a claim you are about to sign.

Manuscript stage AI can help with Stays with you Structure and outline Proposing sections for the venue's format Deciding what the central claim is Drafting First-pass prose from your notes and tables Checking each number and each claim against the data Figures Plot scripts and caption drafts Confirming that each figure shows what its caption says References Formatting and consistency Confirming each cited source exists and says what is claimed Submission Checklists against venue requirements Authorship decisions and disclosure of AI use

Table 5. Where the work divides in manuscript preparation.

A practical technique for the drafting row is a claim audit. Extract every sentence of the draft that contains a number, a comparison, or a causal verb such as "achieves", "reduces", or "because", and write each as a row of a table with its source: a cell in the results table, a figure, or a cited paper. A claim with no source is either cut or sent back to the analysis. In the abstract example, the audit lists "nearly 10-bit resolution" against the source "9.26 bits", and the mismatch is visible at once. Two further matters sit with you alone: whether and how to disclose AI assistance, which venues and institutions increasingly specify in their policies, and the author list, which carries accountability that a tool cannot hold. Both are developed in Chapter 15 and Chapter 18.

Table 6. A one-line summary of each task.

Before the next exercise, three terms need to be fixed, because the activity asks you to place each task in one of three groups. A task is AI drafts, you verify when a model can produce a first version and you can check the result cheaply. A task is You decide, AI assists when the model can supply options or analysis but the choice depends on knowledge and judgment that is yours. A task is You do directly when responsibility, commitment, or certification cannot be handed off at all.

docs.title: The Research Pipeline, Productivity, and Reproducibility
docs.text:
The five tasks are not independent. A research pipeline is the chaining of tasks so that the output of each becomes the input of the next, usually with loops: analysis sends you back to the question, and writing sends you back to analysis. Seeing the work as a pipeline has a practical consequence. The overall trustworthiness of a pipeline is bounded by its weakest stage, and the weakest stage is often the least glamorous. In the running example, a mis-specified record length at the measurement stage would corrupt the analysis, the figures, and the abstract, and no amount of polish downstream would repair it.

A short calculation shows how errors compound. Suppose, illustratively, that each of the five stages has a 90% chance of being free of consequential error. The chance that the whole pipeline is clean is 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59, so roughly four runs in ten would carry some error to the end. Raising any single stage to 99% helps only a little, while a verification step at each handoff attacks the product directly. This is the quantitative reason the book spends as much effort on checking as on generating.

The reason to bring AI into a pipeline is research productivity: the quantity of validated research output produced per unit of researcher time. The word validated is doing the work. A worked example, with illustrative numbers, shows why. A manual literature review of a subtopic takes 40 hours. With an assistant, the first pass takes 12 hours, and 4 further hours are spent verifying citations and reading the key sources. The productivity ratio is 40 / (12 + 4) = 2.5. If verification is skipped, the apparent ratio is 40 / 12 ≈ 3.3, but that figure is counterfeit: the missing 4 hours would have caught the fabricated or misattributed sources, and a single one of them in a submitted paper costs far more than the saving. Honest productivity accounting includes verification time.

Productivity has a second axis that the ratio hides: what the freed time is spent on. Hours recovered from a literature sweep are valuable only if they go to work that needs you, such as reading the three key papers closely, designing a better experiment, or talking to a collaborator. Used to produce more unverified output, the same hours raise the throughput of the pipeline while lowering the quality of what comes out of it.

Reproducibility is the property that another researcher, or you in six months, can regenerate a reported result from recorded inputs, code, and environment. Reproducibility is a long-standing norm of experimental science. AI adds new inputs that must be recorded, because the output of a model depends on them: the prompt, the name and version of the model, and the settings used. A model that is silently updated can give a different answer to the same prompt next month.

The following record shows one way to capture these inputs. The model and version fields identify the system, temperature is a setting that controls how random the output is (0 is the most deterministic), and input_files names the data the output was derived from.

date: 2026-10-15
task: draft search strings for ADC literature search
model: example-assistant
version: 2026-09-snapshot
temperature: 0
prompt_file: prompts/adc-search-strings-v1.txt
input_files: []
output_file: outputs/adc-search-strings-v1.md
reviewed_by: researcher initials, date

A few lines like these, kept next to the output, turn an undocumented conversation into a reproducible step. Later chapters build this habit into project files and logs, and Chapter 17 develops verification in depth.

The practical test of reproducibility is blunt: delete the output and regenerate it from the recorded inputs on a clean checkout. For AI-assisted steps there is a second, honest limit. Many hosted models cannot be made fully deterministic, and a retired model version cannot be re-run at all. The remedy is to record the output alongside the inputs, to treat the model as the source of a candidate and not as a step that must be reproduced bit for bit, and to keep the analysis and computation that follow it fully scripted.

A research group is the lab or team within which most of this work happens: an advisor, students, postdocs, and collaborators who share tools, conventions, and a reputation. The unit of adoption for AI is increasingly the group, not the individual. Consider a six-person group in which each member uses a different assistant with different habits. Results are formatted differently, prompts are not shared, and a new student cannot learn the group's practices because there are none. The same group, with a short shared instruction file and a one-page policy on disclosure, gets consistent output and a way to onboard. Chapter 5 shows how to write that file, and Chapter 18 covers group policy.

Group-level choices include which assistants are approved, where instruction files and prompts live in version control, who reviews AI-assisted contributions before they merge into shared results, and how new members learn the conventions. Advisors carry a particular responsibility, because a group's norms about checking are set by what the advisor visibly checks.

docs.title: The Vocabulary of Generative AI
docs.text: The tasks above were described in terms of AI systems without defining them. This section fixes the vocabulary, building from the broadest term to the most specific, because the distinctions among them determine how much you must supervise.

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
Generative AI is the class of machine learning models that learn the statistical structure of a body of data and use it to produce new samples of the same kind: text, source code, images, audio, or structured data such as circuit netlists. It is contrasted with discriminative models, which map an input to a label or a number.

A worked example separates the two. A discriminative model shown a schematic might answer "this is a common-source amplifier", a label drawn from a fixed set. A generative model, given a request for a common-source amplifier with a specified gain, produces a candidate netlist: new text that did not exist before. The second capability is what makes generative systems useful as drafting tools, and it is also what makes them dangerous, because a generated artifact is a plausible sample and not a derivation.

Two consequences follow for how you use it. First, generation is sampling: the model draws from a probability distribution over possible outputs, so the same request can return different artifacts, and a setting called temperature controls how widely it draws. Second, because correctness is not part of the generation process, correctness must be supplied by a separate test. Electrical engineering is unusually well placed for this, since many generated artifacts can be mechanically checked: a netlist can be simulated, a testbench can be run against a known-good design, a script can be executed on a case with a known answer. The productive pattern is generate and test: let the model produce candidates cheaply, and let simulation or measurement decide which survive. Where no test exists, as with a literature summary or an argument, the burden of checking falls on your own reading.

Discriminative model Generative model Output A label or a value New content of the same kind as the training data Example in EE Classify a waveform as clipped or clean Draft a testbench or a netlist Typical failure Wrong label A plausible but wrong artifact How you check it Compare with ground truth Execute, simulate, or inspect it

Table 7. Discriminative and generative models.

docs.title: Large Language Models
docs.text:
A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on very large collections of text and source code to predict the next unit of text, called a token, given the preceding tokens. A token is a fragment of text, often a word or part of a word. Repeated prediction, one token after another, produces sentences, programs, and tables. The word large refers to the scale of both the training data and the number of learned parameters, and scale is what gave these models their breadth.

A simplified illustration, with invented probabilities, shows the mechanism. Given the prefix "The input impedance of an ideal operational amplifier is", a model assigns a probability to each candidate next token and then selects among them.

Candidate next token Illustrative probability "infinite" 0.78 "very" 0.11 "high" 0.07 "zero" 0.01 anything else 0.03

Table 8. Illustrative next-token probabilities (invented for exposition).

The model is not looking up a fact. It is reproducing the pattern of text it has seen, and when the pattern is dense and consistent, as it is for this textbook fact, the output is right. When the pattern is thin or contradictory, the same mechanism produces fluent text that is false. This failure is called hallucination.

Fluent Does Not Mean True

A model will happily invent a citation with realistic authors, a plausible journal, and a DOI that goes nowhere. Look up every reference you intend to cite, by its DOI or title, in a database you trust, before it goes into a draft.

Chapter 2 explains tokens, context windows, and the causes of hallucination in detail. For now, the working rule is that an LLM is a pattern generator whose outputs are hypotheses until checked.

Three limits of a language model are worth carrying into every later chapter. It has a knowledge cutoff: it has seen nothing published after its training data was assembled, so recent papers, new device families, and updated standards may be absent or wrong. It has a context window: it can attend to only a limited amount of text at once, so a long thesis chapter pasted in whole may be partly ignored. And it is not deterministic by default: the same prompt can return different answers on different days. A worked case illustrates the first. Asked for the quiescent current of a specific voltage regulator by part number, a model may return a confident figure that is plausible for the device class and wrong for the part. The remedy is to supply the datasheet and ask the model to answer only from it, which turns recall into reading and lets you check the answer against a page.

docs.title: AI Assistants
docs.text:
An AI assistant is an application that places an LLM behind a conversational interface. You send a request, optionally with files or pasted text, and the assistant returns a reply, one turn at a time. It carries the conversation history so that follow-ups make sense, and it follows instructions given at the start of the session. What defines an assistant is that you drive: each action in the world is taken by you.

The debugging example makes this concrete. A script fails with an error message. You paste the script and the error into an assistant, which explains the likely cause and returns a corrected version. You copy the fix into your editor, run it yourself, observe the new result, and report back. The assistant never ran the code and never saw the outcome except through your description. This is powerful and cheap to supervise: the assistant cannot do anything you did not do.

Several features of assistants matter in research use. A system prompt or custom-instruction field lets you set standing context, such as your field, preferred units, and the rule that every claim must carry a source, so that you do not retype it. Conversation history means the assistant can build on earlier turns, but it also means that early mistakes persist and that a long session can drift. Most assistants accept files or pasted text, which turns them into readers of your own material. Vendors can also give them tools such as web search or a code interpreter, which blurs the line toward agents; the practical test is whether the system chooses and takes actions in sequence without you prompting each one. For the purposes of this book, an assistant is the right tool when the task is a single, reviewable transformation: explain this, rewrite that, draft this section, convert this format. It is the wrong tool when the task needs many steps whose intermediate results you do not want to relay by hand.

docs.title: AI Agents
docs.text:
An AI agent is a system that uses an LLM to decide which actions to take, invokes tools to take them, observes the results, and repeats until a goal is reached or it stops to ask. Four elements define one: a goal, a set of tools it can call (such as reading files, running code, or searching the web), a loop that alternates deciding and acting, and some form of memory of what has happened.

Return to the same failing script. An agent given the goal "make the test pass" opens the file, runs the test, reads the error, edits the code, reruns the test, and repeats until the test passes or a limit is reached, reporting what it did. You did not copy anything or run anything. That saves your time, and it changes the risk. The agent took actions, including modifying files, that you did not individually approve, and the success it reports is only as trustworthy as the test it was told to satisfy.

Tools are the point of leverage and the point of risk. A file-reading tool lets an agent work from your actual project instead of a description of it; a code-execution tool lets it test its own work; a web tool lets it retrieve sources. Each tool also defines what can go wrong: a shell tool can delete files, and a network tool can send data out of your institution. Limits therefore attach to tools, not to the model: which directories an agent can write to, which commands it may run, and how many steps it may take before it must stop and report. Chapter 8 treats these controls in detail.

AI assistant AI agent Who takes actions in the world You The system, through tools Unit of work One reply to one request A multi-step task toward a goal What you review The reply, before you use it The plan, the actions taken, and the final result Main risk Accepting a wrong reply Actions with side effects you did not see Typical supervision Read and apply Set limits, log, and check afterward

Table 9. Assistant and agent compared.

The Difference Is Who Closes the Loop

An assistant answers and waits for you to act. An agent acts, looks at what happened, and acts again. Think of it like this: every step an agent takes without you is a step you must be able to audit afterward.

Before the next exercise, note the chain of terms the chapter has built: generative AI is the broad class, an LLM is a generative model specialized for language, an assistant wraps an LLM in a conversational interface, and an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant.

docs.title: Agentic Research
docs.text:
Agentic research is research conducted by delegating multi-step tasks to AI agents, with the researcher setting goals, defining limits, and verifying results. It is the combination of the task vocabulary and the agent vocabulary of this chapter: the five tasks, performed in part by systems that act.

A worked example shows the scale of the change. Before leaving for the evening, you give an agent the goal "find, deduplicate, and summarize every paper from the last three years on SAR ADCs below 100 µW", with the instruction to record each source's DOI and to flag anything it could not verify. In the morning you do not receive an answer. You receive a draft annotated list, a log of what was searched, and a list of items marked unverified. The remaining work, deciding which items matter and checking the flagged ones, is faster and better directed than starting from nothing.

Two cautions keep the example honest. The agent's list is a search result, not a literature review: its coverage depends on the databases it could reach and the terms it chose, and a gap in the list is invisible unless you probe for it with a second, differently phrased sweep or with a known paper that should have appeared. And the log is only evidence of what the agent says it did; sampling a few entries and reproducing them yourself is how you establish that the log can be trusted. A newer class of always-on personal agents extends this pattern to agents that keep their own cloud computer and work continuously; Chapter 19 and the Personal Agents appendix cover them and the questions they raise.

docs.title: Directing Agents Responsibly
docs.text: Using agents well is a skill with two halves: dividing the work so that each part can be handed off and checked, and placing yourself in the work at the points where your judgment matters most. The next two concepts are those halves.

docs.title: Task Decomposition
docs.text:
Task decomposition is the breaking of a goal into subtasks small enough to specify, delegate, and verify, together with the dependencies among them. A subtask is well formed when it has a clear input, a limited scope, an output you can check, and a known place in the order of work. Decomposition is the most transferable skill in this book, because it determines what you can safely hand to an agent and what you cannot.

A worked example uses the running project. The goal is to compare the measured and simulated ENOB of two ADC designs. Stated that way, it is not a task an agent can be given, because it does not say what to do first. Decomposed, it becomes six subtasks, shown with their prerequisites in Table 10.

ID Subtask Output you can check Prerequisite S1 Define the ENOB measurement procedure: input frequency, amplitude, and record length A one-page procedure none S2 Simulate both designs using the procedure Two simulated output records S1 S3 Measure both fabricated chips using the procedure Two measured output records S1 S4 Compute ENOB from each simulated record Two simulated ENOB values S2 S5 Compute ENOB from each measured record Two measured ENOB values S3 S6 Compare simulated and measured ENOB and explain differences A comparison table and a short explanation S4, S5

Table 10. The ADC comparison goal decomposed into six subtasks.

Two properties are worth noticing. S2 and S3 can proceed in either order or in parallel, because both depend only on S1. And each subtask names an output you can inspect, which is what lets you hand it to an agent and later verify it without redoing it.

The criteria for a well-formed subtask can be applied as a checklist. Does it have a stated input? Does it produce an artifact you could inspect, not just an activity? Is its scope small enough that a failure is easy to localize? Are its prerequisites explicit? And can it be accepted or rejected without redoing it? A subtask that fails the second question, such as "think about the measurement", is an intention and not a task. A subtask that fails the third, such as "build the whole analysis toolchain", hides several tasks inside one and makes failure ambiguous. Decomposition also exposes hidden dependencies: in the example, nobody can compute a measured ENOB before the chips are measured, and nothing can be measured before the procedure fixes the record length. Discovering that on paper costs minutes; discovering it in the lab costs a fabrication cycle.

If Decomposition Feels Vague, That Is Normal

Most people write a first breakdown that is either too coarse to delegate or too fine to bother with, and that is how everyone starts. Work backward from the deliverable: ask what the last step must receive, then what produces that, and repeat until each piece has a checkable output.

The exercise below uses the same goal. You are given eight candidate subtasks, of which six are correct and two are not, and must put the correct ones in a valid order.

Prerequisites: task decomposition, subtask, prerequisite, checkable output, effective number of bits (ENOB) (all defined in the sections "Task Decomposition" and "The Setting: Electrical Engineering Research" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner builds one ordered list from the eight candidates and submits it. The submission is correct when (a) it contains exactly the six subtasks S1 to S6 and neither distractor, and (b) for every subtask in the list, all of its prerequisites appear earlier in the list. Mastery is a correct submission within two submissions. Moving cards before submitting is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A goal such as "do the research" is a subtask. (2) Every subtask must follow a single fixed sequence, when S2 and S3 are independent. (3) A subtask that improves the design belongs in a comparison of measured and simulated ENOB.

Content:

docs.title: Human in the Loop
docs.text:
Human in the loop is a design in which a person reviews, approves, or steers an automated process at defined points, retaining the ability to stop it. It is not a single setting. Systems differ in where the human sits and how often they must act.

Position What the human does Suitable when In the loop Approves each consequential action before it runs Actions are irreversible or leave your control On the loop Monitors a log and can interrupt Actions are reversible and the volume is high Out of the loop Reviews only the final result The output is cheap to check and the process cannot cause harm

Table 11. Three positions of a person relative to an automated process.

Choosing the position is a judgment about cost. Three questions settle most cases. Is the action reversible? Does the output leave your control, by being sent, published, or used to commit resources? And does the output become a reported result, so that an error in it propagates into your claims? If the answer to any is yes, a review point belongs before the output is used. If none is, the process can usually run with lighter supervision.

A worked example applies the questions to an analysis agent working on your measured data. Suppose the agent proposes to overwrite the raw measurement files with cleaned versions. The action is irreversible, so the question is settled: stop and require approval, and better still, instruct the agent to write cleaned data to a new file so the original is never at risk. Now suppose the agent proposes to rename a column in a copy of the file. The action is reversible, the copy stays with you, and the change is trivially visible. No approval is needed, and asking for one would only teach you to click through requests.

A known weakness of review is automation bias: the tendency to accept the output of an automated system with less scrutiny than the same output from a person, particularly when the system has been right many times before. A reviewer who has approved fifty correct outputs approves the fifty-first by habit. Designs that counter it ask the reviewer to do something that cannot be done by habit: state the expected value before seeing the output, check a random sample against the source rather than the first few items, or write a short reason for approval. Review that has become a click is a loop in name only.

Ask the Question Every Time

Before accepting any output, ask, "How would you check that?" If the honest answer is "I wouldn't", it is not ready to use. If you can name the check and it is cheap, run it.

The exercise below gives you eight steps an agent might take in an analysis workflow and asks you to judge which of them need your review before the output is used.

Prerequisites: human in the loop, reversible and irreversible actions, output that leaves your control, output that becomes a reported result (all defined in the section "Human in the Loop" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight agent steps, the learner commits one of two judgments, "Review required" or "No review needed", and selects the main reason from three offered reasons. A step is correct when the judgment matches the Review column of the Content table. Mastery is 7 of 8 judgments correct on the first run. Reading the three questions listed in the Rules is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every agent action needs review, so review is never a choice. (2) A step that looks harmless needs no review even when it is irreversible. (3) A step that only drafts something is safe to send without review.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluating requires judging against criteria and justifying the judgment. The learner applies three explicit criteria to eight cases and must pick the reason for the judgment, which separates a correct guess from a correct decision.

Content:

The three criteria (shown at all times):

Criterion Question Reversibility Is the action irreversible? Outward effect Does the output leave your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources? Reported result Does the output become a result you will report?

A step requires review when at least one criterion applies.

The eight agent steps:

# Agent step shown to the learner Review Main reason Why (shown as feedback) 1 The agent lists 20 candidate keywords for a literature search No review needed No criterion applies A poor keyword only wastes one search, and you see it at once 2 The agent reports "Smith 2021 shows 12-bit ENOB at 40 µW" with a citation Review required Reported result The claim and the citation may be fabricated, and would enter your paper 3 The agent renames a column header in a copy of the data file No review needed No criterion applies The change is reversible, the original is preserved, and it is easy to see 4 The agent runs a script that overwrites the raw measurement files Review required Reversibility Raw data lost this way cannot be recovered 5 The agent computes ENOB = 10.3 from your data and says it will go in the abstract Review required Reported result A number entering a manuscript must be checked independently 6 The agent sends an email asking a collaborator for a dataset Review required Outward effect Sending cannot be undone and the message speaks for you 7 The agent drafts the same email and leaves it unsent in the drafts folder No review needed No criterion applies Nothing leaves your control until you send it 8 The agent changes a simulation parameter on a scratch branch under version control No review needed No criterion applies The change is reversible and isolated from the main work

Rules: A step is "Review required" when at least one of the three criteria applies, and "No review needed" when none applies. The score counts steps where the judgment matches the Review column. The reason offered for each step is one of "Reversibility", "Outward effect", or "Reported result", plus "No criterion applies" for steps that need no review. Mastery requires a score >= 7 of 8. Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the three criteria and one agent step at a time.
  2. The learner judges the step "Review required" or "No review needed" and selects the main reason. The learner commits both.
  3. The sim shows whether the judgment matched, the Why sentence, and the correct reason.
  4. After eight steps, the learner sees the score and the steps judged incorrectly with their Why sentences.
  5. The learner may run again with a reshuffled order.

Feedback: Eight steps, one commit per step, no change after commit. A correct judgment with the correct reason shows "Correct". A correct judgment with the wrong reason shows "Right decision, different reason" and the correct reason. An incorrect judgment shows "Not quite", the Why sentence, and the correct judgment. The score counts judgments only, and is shown as "n of 8". Answers are revealed after each commit.
