docs.title: The Researcher as Orchestrator
docs.text:
The researcher as orchestrator is the organizing idea of this book: instead of performing every task personally, the researcher directs a team of agents, sets direction, supplies domain judgment, resolves conflicts among them, and decides what is true. The model developed in later chapters assigns roughly 20 planning agents, which explore, decompose, and specify, and 10 execution agents, which write code, run analyses, and prepare figures. The numbers are a design target, not a law; they express the idea that planning is cheap to parallelize and execution needs closer supervision.

In the running example, the orchestrator's day might look like this. Several planning agents each take a different part of the ADC comparison: one surveys architectures, one drafts the measurement procedure (S1), one proposes how to estimate uncertainty. You read their outputs, resolve a disagreement between two of them about record length by reasoning from the converter's bandwidth, and approve the procedure. Execution agents then run the simulations (S2), compute simulated ENOB (S4), and, when the chips are measured, the measured ENOB (S5). You are not typing the scripts. You are choosing what gets run, checking what comes back against the test oracle from the coding section, and signing the result. The work has not become easier so much as it has moved: from production to direction and verification.

The orchestrator's scarcest resource is attention, not typing speed. Each additional agent adds output to review, so the useful size of a team is set by how much you can verify, not by how many agents you can launch. Chapters 9 and 10 develop roles, handoffs, and the supervision techniques that keep a team of this kind honest.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Research in electrical engineering is a workflow of repeatable tasks with checkable outputs, and AI systems now absorb a substantial share of the procedural layer. The researcher's job is to supply what the workflow cannot: the question, the domain judgment, and the accountability.

The main points to carry forward:

  • The workflow consists of five everyday tasks (literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, manuscript preparation) chained into a pipeline whose trustworthiness is bounded by its weakest stage.
  • A precise research question with a metric and a threshold is the cheapest quality control available when using AI.
  • Generative AI, large language models, assistants, and agents form a chain; an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant, and with them, actions you did not individually approve.
  • LLM output is a hypothesis until checked, because fluent text can be false.
  • Productivity must include verification time, and reproducibility now includes recording prompts, models, and settings.
  • Task decomposition into subtasks with checkable outputs is what makes delegation safe.
  • Human review belongs where an action is irreversible, leaves your control, or becomes a reported result.
  • The researcher as orchestrator directs and verifies; accountability for the science stays with you.

You Have the Map

You can now name the five research tasks, tell an assistant from an agent by who closes the loop, and decide where a human review point belongs. That is the vocabulary and the habit of checking that the rest of this book builds on.

The next chapter looks inside the models themselves, so that the failure modes introduced here, hallucination in particular, become something you can reason about rather than something that surprises you. Round up the evidence, and bring the question you would most like an agent to help with.

docs.title: Learning Graph for AI for EE Research
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
The 379 concepts in the AI for EE Research learning graph are organized into 17 categories. Each concept has exactly one primary category, identified by a 3-6 letter TaxonomyID that is used in learning-graph.csv and as the group key in learning-graph.json. The categories follow the course's teaching order: foundations first, then how models work, then the Markdown and skill building blocks, then agents and orchestration, then the five research tasks, and finally verification, ethics, and the capstone. The always-on personal agents and personal knowledge graph categories were added afterward and are numbered last so that existing concept IDs did not change.

No category holds more than 10% of the concepts, well under the 30% ceiling.

docs.text: Run the From Generative AI to Agent MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Four terms appear in a row as a chain: Generative AI, Large Language Model, AI Assistant, and AI Agent, joined by three links. The question on screen is What changes at each step from generative AI to an AI agent?

Each link asks what the second term adds to the first. You choose one of four options and commit. Three of the options are common misconceptions, such as the idea that a larger model or a friendlier tone is what turns an assistant into an agent. After each commit the sim reveals the correct capability, and if you chose a distractor it explains why that choice belongs somewhere else in the chain.

The chain ends with the point the chapter makes: an AI agent is an AI assistant plus tools and a loop. It acts, observes the result, and chooses the next step.

You can open any node at any time to read its definition. Opening a node is exploration and is not scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any node in the diagram, or use the Open a node buttons below it, to read that term's definition. This step is optional and is not scored.
  2. Look at the exercise panel. It shows Link 1 of 3: Generative AI → Large Language Model and asks What does the second term add to the first?
  3. Select one of the four options, then press Commit answer. You can also use the arrow keys to move between options and press Enter to commit.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows "Correct" and the correct option. An incorrect choice shows why that option does not fit this link, followed by the correct option. You cannot change an answer after you commit it.
  5. Press Next link to move on. A link cannot be answered until the previous link has been answered. Each answered link is marked in the diagram with a check mark (correct) or an X (incorrect).
  6. After the third link the panel shows your final score as n of 3 correct. Mastery is 3 of 3.
  7. Press Restart at any time to begin a new run. The order of the options is reshuffled on every run.

docs.title: Research Task Decomposition Builder
docs.text: Run the Research Task Decomposition Builder MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Task decomposition breaks a research goal into subtasks that each have a checkable output and explicit prerequisites. This MicroSim asks you to apply two criteria to one concrete goal from Chapter 1:

Goal: Compare the measured and simulated ENOB of two ADC designs.

You see eight candidate subtask cards, labeled A to H in a shuffled order. Six of them are the subtasks S1 to S6 that decompose the goal. The other two are distractors: one is not a subtask at all, and one is outside the scope of the goal. Your job is to build one ordered list that contains exactly the six subtasks, in an order where every subtask comes after all of its prerequisites.

A submission is valid when:

  • all six subtasks S1 to S6 are present and neither distractor is present, and
  • for every subtask, each of its prerequisites appears at an earlier position. S2 and S3 may appear in either order. S4 must appear after S2, and S5 after S3. S6 must appear after both S4 and S5.

When you press Check Order, the sim reports every problem it finds: a card that does not belong (with its "Why" sentence), a required subtask that is missing, or a card placed before its prerequisite (naming both cards and giving the "Why" sentence). You have two submissions. After a correct submission, or after the second submission, the answer and the reason for every card are shown, together with the result: Correct within n submission(s) or Not yet correct.

Learning objective: apply the criteria of a checkable output and a valid order to select six well-formed subtasks from eight candidates and sequence them so every prerequisite precedes its dependent.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the goal and the eight cards. The question on screen is Which of these are well-formed subtasks for this goal, and in what order?
  2. Pick a card in the drop-down list below the drawing. The picked card is outlined in dark blue.
  3. Press Add Card to put it at the end of your sequence. A card in the sequence is shaded and shows its position, for example #3, and the drop-down list shows the same number.
  4. To reorder, pick a card that is already in the sequence and press Move Earlier to move it up one position. When a card in the sequence is picked, the add button reads Remove Card; press it to take the card out, then add it again at the end. Any order can be built with these two moves.
  5. Press Check Order to submit. An empty sequence is rejected and does not use a submission. A sequence with fewer than six cards is reported as incomplete.
  6. Read the feedback. Every problem is listed with its reason. On a narrow screen, the feedback opens on its own page; press Next Page to read more, and pick or edit a card to return to the cards.
  7. Revise the sequence and press Check Order a second time if needed. After a correct submission or the second submission, the answer is shown: the six subtasks in a valid order and the two distractors, each with its reason. Use Next Page if the answer does not fit on one page.
  8. Start Over empties the sequence. Before the answer is shown, it keeps the submissions you have used. After the answer is shown, it starts a new attempt with the cards reshuffled and two new submissions; earlier results stay on the status line.

1. Exploration (5 min): Before adding any card, read the eight cards and apply the checklist from the chapter to each one: Does it have a stated input? Does it produce an artifact you could inspect? Is its scope small enough that a failure is easy to localize? Mark the two cards that fail. Then work backward from the deliverable: ask what the last subtask must receive, then what produces that, and sketch the order on paper.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Build the sequence with Add Card, Move Earlier, and Remove Card, and submit it with Check Order. If the feedback lists problems, read each "Why" sentence and decide whether it is a membership error (a distractor or a missing subtask) or an ordering error (a card before its prerequisite). Fix only what the feedback names and submit a second time. Notice that S2 and S3 can be swapped without breaking the order, because both depend only on S1.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Record the result shown after the answer is revealed. Then, without the sim, write a decomposition of a goal from your own research into four to six subtasks, give each a checkable output, list its prerequisites, and mark which subtasks are independent of each other and could run in parallel.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: a correct submission within two submissions, shown as Correct within 1 submission or Correct within 2 submissions. Not yet correct after the second submission means mastery is not yet shown.
  • The learner can explain why each distractor is excluded: "Do the research on the ADC" has no checkable output and no defined scope, and "Improve the ADC until its ENOB reaches 9.5 bits" changes the design instead of comparing ENOB.
  • The learner can state the prerequisite of each subtask and explain why S2 and S3 may appear in either order.
  • Moving cards before submitting, and reading the revealed answer, are exploration, not evidence of mastery.

docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "Task Decomposition" defines a well-formed subtask and is the source of the goal, the six subtasks S1 to S6 (Table 10), and their prerequisites.

docs.title: Research Task Sorter
docs.text: Run the Research Task Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Not every research task should be handed to a model, and not every task should be kept away from one. This MicroSim asks you to differentiate ten research tasks by the kind of check or judgment they need, not by how technical they sound. Each task belongs in exactly one of three groups:

Group Meaning AI drafts, you verify A model can produce a first version, and you can check the result cheaply You decide, AI assists A model can supply options or analysis; the choice depends on your knowledge and judgment You do directly Responsibility, commitment, or certification that cannot be handed off

The ten task cards come from the five everyday research tasks in Chapter 1: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, and manuscript preparation. After each placement the sim tells you whether it matched the answer key, gives a one-sentence reason, and, when you missed, names the correct group. The goal is to match the answer key on at least 8 of 10 cards.

Learning objective: differentiate ten research tasks into "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly", matching the answer key in at least 8 of 10 tasks.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task card in the dark-blue box and the three group definitions below it. The question on screen is Who should do this task: the model, you assisted, or only you?
  2. Press the button with the name of the group you choose. The placement is committed at once and cannot be changed.
  3. Read the feedback. Correct (with a check mark) or Not quite (with an X) is followed by the "Why" sentence, and a miss also shows the correct group. The correct group is outlined and marked with a check mark; a wrong pick is marked with an X.
  4. Press Next Card to continue. The Placed count on each group shows how many cards you have put there in this run.
  5. After the tenth card, press See Score. The summary shows n of 10 correct, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and every card you placed incorrectly with its correct group and "Why" sentence. If the list is long, press More Missed Cards to page through it.
  6. Press Run Again to play a new run with the cards reshuffled. The score of every run stays on screen so you can see whether you improved.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The five everyday research tasks (literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, manuscript preparation) from the section "The Five Everyday Research Tasks" in Chapter 1
  • The definitions of the three groups "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly"
  • Basic familiarity with lab measurement, simulation, and paper-writing workflows in electrical engineering

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Before placing any card, read the three group definitions and write down, in one phrase each, the test you will use to tell them apart (for example: "Can I check the output cheaply?", "Does the choice depend on what only I know?", "Does it carry my signature or commitment?"). Then play one run without stopping to think too long, and note which cards surprised you.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Review the list of missed cards on the summary screen. For each miss, read the "Why" sentence and decide which of your three tests you applied incorrectly. Compare two cards that sound similar but fall in different groups, such as "Draft an abstract from a table of measured results" (AI drafts, you verify) and "Certify before submission that the reported measurements were taken and not generated" (You do directly), and explain in a sentence what separates them.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Press Run Again and sort the reshuffled cards. Record both run scores. Then write one new task from your own research that would belong in each group, and justify each placement with a sentence in the style of the "Why" feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: at least 8 of 10 placements match the answer key on the first run. The score of the second (reshuffled) run shows whether the criteria transferred.
  • The learner can state, for any missed card, why the answer-key group is correct, using the distinction between cheap verification, judgment that depends on the researcher's knowledge, and responsibility that cannot be delegated.
  • The learner's three self-written tasks are each placed in a defensible group with a one-sentence justification.
  • Reading the feedback and reviewing the missed-card list are exploration, not evidence of mastery.

docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "The Five Everyday Research Tasks" defines the three groups and is the source of all ten task cards and their answer key.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This diagram turns Table 1 of Chapter 1 into a flowchart. The running example follows a doctoral student designing a low-power SAR ADC through five stages. Each box is a stage, and each arrow carries the artifact that the stage hands to the next one. The example is illustrative and not drawn from a published study.

docs.title: Workflow Steps
docs.text:
1. Find what is known takes a topic and a gap and produces a reading list with citations.
  2. Frame the question turns the reading list and a design goal into one falsifiable question statement.
  3. Build and measure uses the question and a design to produce netlists, scripts, and raw data files.
  4. Analyze turns the raw data files into result tables and plots with uncertainty.
  5. Communicate turns the result tables and plots into manuscript source and figures.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over any box to see its input, output, and handoff artifact in the right panel.
  2. Hover over an arrow label to read what that artifact is and which stages it connects.
  3. Click each box. A clicked box gets a green outline, and the counter above the panel shows how many of the seven boxes you have clicked. With the keyboard, press Tab to reach a box and Enter or Space to click it.
  4. Click all seven boxes to fire the confetti cannon once. It does not fire before then, and it does not fire again. Confetti is skipped if your system requests reduced motion.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will describe the input, output, and handoff artifact of each of the five research workflow stages (Bloom: Understand, verb: describe).

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Cover the right panel and name the handoff artifact on each arrow from memory. Then hover to check. For one arrow, say what would go wrong downstream if that artifact contained an unnoticed error.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the learner name the artifact passed between each pair of adjacent stages?
  • Can the learner explain why a handoff is where quality is either confirmed or silently lost?

docs.title: Review Checkpoint Judge
docs.text: Run the Review Checkpoint Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An agent that can act on your files, send messages, and compute results will take many steps you did not individually approve. Asking for approval on every step teaches you to click through requests; asking for none lets an irreversible or public mistake through. This MicroSim asks you to judge where a human review checkpoint belongs, using three criteria from Chapter 1 that stay on screen the whole time:

Criterion Question Reversibility Is the action irreversible? Outward effect Does the output leave your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources? Reported result Does the output become a result you will report?

A step requires review when at least one criterion applies.

You see eight agent steps from an analysis workflow, one at a time and in a new shuffled order on every run. For each step you commit two things together: a judgment, Review required or No review needed, and the main reason, which is one of the three criteria or No criterion applies. Choosing the reason separates a correct decision from a correct guess. Four of the eight steps require review and four do not.

Learning objective: judge, for each of eight agent steps in an analysis workflow, whether a human review checkpoint is required before its output is used, agreeing with the answer key on at least 7 of 8 steps.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the three criteria at the top and the agent step in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Does this output need your review before it is used?
  2. Choose the main reason in the drop-down list below the drawing: Reversibility, Outward effect, Reported result, or No criterion applies. If you press a judgment button without choosing a reason, the sim asks you to choose one first and nothing is recorded.
  3. Press Review required or No review needed. The judgment and the reason are committed together and cannot be changed.
  4. Read the feedback. Correct means both the judgment and the reason match the answer key. Right decision, different reason means the judgment matches but the reason does not; the correct reason is shown. Not quite means the judgment does not match; the correct judgment is shown. The "Why" sentence appears after every commit, and the criterion that is the main reason is marked Main reason with a check mark.
  5. Press Next Step to continue. After the eighth step, press See Score. The summary shows the score as n of 8 (it counts judgments only), whether you reached mastery (7 of 8), and every step judged incorrectly with its "Why" sentence. If the list is long, press More Missed Steps to page through it.
  6. Press Run Again to judge the eight steps again in a reshuffled order. The score of every run stays on screen.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Human in the loop: the three positions of a person relative to an automated process (in the loop, on the loop, out of the loop), from the section "Human in the Loop" in Chapter 1
  • Reversible and irreversible actions
  • Output that leaves your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources
  • Output that becomes a reported result
  • The idea of an agent as an assistant with tools and a loop, which can take actions you did not individually approve

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Read the three criteria and restate each one as a yes/no test you could apply in under ten seconds. Then judge the first step without hurrying, and read the "Why" sentence and the marked main reason before pressing Next Step. Reading the criteria is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Finish the run. On the summary screen, for each step judged incorrectly, name the criterion you applied (or failed to apply) and explain the miss using the "Why" sentence. Compare two pairs that look alike but are judged differently: the agent sends an email versus drafts the same email and leaves it unsent, and the agent overwrites the raw measurement files versus renames a column header in a copy of the data file. Write one sentence for each pair saying which criterion separates them.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Press Run Again and judge the reshuffled steps. Record the first-run and second-run scores and how many steps showed Right decision, different reason. Then describe one agent step from your own research workflow, judge it, and name its main reason in the style of the "Why" feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: at least 7 of 8 judgments match the answer key on the first run. The score counts judgments only.
  • The learner names the correct main reason for each step that requires review (Reversibility, Outward effect, or Reported result) and gives "No criterion applies" for the four steps that do not. A "Right decision, different reason" result shows a judgment that is not yet backed by the right criterion.
  • The learner explains, for any missed step, why the answer-key judgment is correct using the three criteria.
  • The learner's own example step is judged with a defensible reason.
  • Common misconceptions to listen for: every agent action needs review, so review is never a choice; a step that looks harmless needs no review even when it is irreversible; a step that only drafts something is safe to send without review.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "Human in the Loop" states the three review criteria (reversibility, outward effect, reported result) and is the source of the eight agent steps and their answer key.
